Produce (noun) means fresh fruits and vegetables, especially ones that are grown on a farm and sold for people to eat.

That's the heart of it. When a grocery store has a section full of apples, tomatoes, lettuce, carrots, and bananas — that entire section is called the produce section. Everything in it, collectively, is called "produce."

Think of it this way: a farmer grows things in the soil or on trees. Those fresh, natural, edible things — before they get processed, cooked, canned, or packaged into something else — are "produce."

Produce almost always refers to fresh items. Here is what typically falls under this word:

Fruits — apples, mangoes, strawberries, grapes, oranges, watermelons, peaches, and so on.

Vegetables — broccoli, spinach, potatoes, onions, peppers, cucumbers, zucchini, and so on.

Herbs — fresh basil, parsley, cilantro, and mint are often included too, since they are fresh and farm-grown.

Occasionally, you might also hear "produce" used to include other raw, farm-fresh items like mushrooms or sometimes even fresh-cut flowers at a farmer's market stall, since these are also grown and sold fresh. However, in everyday usage, fruits and vegetables are the clear core meaning.
What Does NOT Count as Produce?

This boundary is important. Produce specifically means fresh and unprocessed. So the following things are generally not called produce:

  • Canned tomatoes (they have been processed)
  • Frozen peas (they are no longer fresh)
  • Dried fruits like raisins (processed by drying)
  • Bread, meat, dairy, or packaged snacks

If a vegetable has been turned into something else — a jar of tomato sauce, a bag of frozen corn — it stops being "produce" and becomes a packaged or processed food product.

"Produce" as a noun is an uncountable noun (also called a mass noun). This means:

  • You cannot say "a produce" or "two produces." ❌
  • You can say "some produce," "fresh produce," "local produce," or just "produce." ✅

It works like the word "water" or "music" — you refer to it as a whole, not as individual countable units.

Examples:

  • "I need to buy some produce for dinner."
  • "The produce at this farmer's market is incredibly fresh."
  • "She filled her basket with produce."
  • "The store receives a shipment of produce every morning."

Notice that you use it with "some," with adjectives, or on its own — but never with "a" or counted with numbers.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

In grocery stores: Almost every supermarket has a dedicated "produce section" or "produce aisle." This is the area — usually near the entrance — where all the fresh fruits and vegetables are displayed, often misted with water to keep them fresh.

At farmer's markets: People go to farmer's markets to buy fresh, locally-grown produce directly from the farmers who grew it.

In cooking and recipes: Food writers and cooks often say things like "use the freshest produce you can find" or "seasonal produce" (meaning fruits and vegetables that are naturally available during a particular time of year).

In farming and agriculture: Farmers talk about their "produce" to mean what they have grown and are ready to sell.

In news and business: You might read headlines like "Rising prices affect fresh produce" or "Demand for organic produce has grown."

Knowing the word alone is not enough — here are the most common and useful phrases built around it:

Fresh produce — the most common phrase; emphasizes that the fruits and vegetables are not frozen or canned. "Always choose fresh produce when possible."

Local produce — fruits and vegetables grown nearby, in your region, rather than shipped from far away. "This restaurant uses only local produce."

Organic produce — fruits and vegetables grown without synthetic pesticides or chemical fertilizers. "Organic produce tends to cost more."

Seasonal produce — whatever fruits or vegetables naturally grow during a particular season. Strawberries in summer, pumpkins in autumn, etc. "Cooking with seasonal produce makes meals taste better and costs less."

Produce section / produce aisle — the part of a grocery store dedicated to fresh fruits and vegetables. "The produce section is usually the first thing you see when you walk into the store."

Produce stand — a small, simple outdoor stall or shop where farmers or vendors sell fresh fruits and vegetables. "We stopped at a produce stand on the side of the road."
One Important Note: Noun vs. Verb

The word "produce" also exists as a verb, meaning "to make or create something." For example: "This factory produces cars." When it is a verb, the stress in pronunciation falls on the second syllable. When it is a noun (the form you are learning here), the stress falls on the first syllable. The meaning is completely different depending on which form is being used. Just remember: noun = fresh fruits and vegetables.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Produce (noun) = the fresh, farm-grown fruits and vegetables you find in the fresh section of a store or market, before they are cooked or processed into anything else.

If you can picture the colourful, fresh, unpackaged section of a grocery store — full of leafy greens, ripe tomatoes, and bright fruits — you are picturing "produce."
